svg.title: Paragraphs or one verse per line?
svg.desc: 2 annotated interface examples with use cases and tradeoffs. Scripture samples are identified by edition.

g.text: Paragraphs or one verse per line?
Poetry is a content structure to preserve in either layout, not a third competing preference.
A · Paragraphs
Luke 15 · BSB
1 Now all the tax collectors and sinners were
gathering around to listen to Jesus. 2 So the
Pharisees and scribes began to grumble: “This
man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” 3
Then Jesus told them this parable:
Aa · Reading settings
Paragraph grouping supports continuous reading; verse
numbers remain available.
Use when: Following an argument or narrative
Consider: Inline numbers can interrupt reading; keep them
subordinate.
B · Verse per line
Luke 15 · BSB
Now all the tax collectors and sinners were
gathering around to listen to Jesus.
So the Pharisees and scribes began to
grumble: “This man welcomes sinners and
eats with them.”
Then Jesus told them this parable:
Aa · Reading settings
A new line makes each verse easier to locate. It does
not turn every verse into a separate thought.
Use when: Finding, discussing or selecting individual verses
Consider: The visual rhythm may imply each verse is a
separate thought.
Original illustrative interfaces · Static controls · Any Scripture samples identify their edition. Sample catalogue and resource details are
illustrative.
